Author: Erin Rossiter
Summary: A Savannah Morning News feature on Grace and Mary Wilkowski, their fast-paced 2003-04 St. Andrew's team, and the sisters' role in the Saints' return to the top of SCISA Class AA.

Transcript:
SISTER, SISTER - SCORE, SCORE
GRACE AND MARY WILKOWSKI HELP TURN ST. ANDREW'S INTO A HIGH-SCORING UNIT.

You might not recognize the game St. Andrew's plays, but the sisters on the basketball court should get your attention.

One quieter than the other, one feeding passes to the next, both aiming their team at a return to the top of SCISA Class AA, Grace and Mary Wilkowski are again dominant.

With eye-popping numbers, the Wilkowskis have helped lead their 9-3 Wilmington Island team to the head of SCISA Region 2-AA with a 5-0 mark heading into tonight's game against Colleton Prep.

But they are doing it in a way no one may have expected.

The team's focus this year is on scoring, whereas last year the Saints focused on controlled possessions, selective shots and conservative dig-in defense.

"Last year, our goals were to play well and to have a limited number of turnovers," said Mary, a 5-foot-11 freshman. "If the score was two to nothing at the end it didn't matter, as long as you come out on the upper side."

The Saints did come out on the upper side, winning the SCISA Class AA title by beating Greenville's Carolina Academy 47-42.

Their transition into a fastbreak offense happened with a few staff changes over the summer, including new coach Kevin Kunst and new point guard Jennifer Moesch, who transferred from St. Vincent's.

"Our other guards are very reliable and consistent but she adds the dimension of spontaneity when she scores," Grace said. "She is very unpredictable for the other team as far as when she is going to take a dive to the basket."

Kunst, who coaches the Saints' football team, asked school administrators if he could lead the team midsummer after former coach and athletic director Deb Morell took a job at Johnson High.

Some of the first changes Kunst made were adding players and changing their offensive style to suit the talents of the smaller players, like 5-foot-9 Grace, as well as the fleet-footed Moesch.

Then, he challenged them to be more offensive-minded.

"Sixty percent from the free-throw line, 60 points," he said, repeating his instructions. "If they can do that, we can beat anybody."

With only six players on the varsity team last year, the Saints were very careful with their shots and stayed conservative on defense.

They scored more than 60 points four times during their 2002-2003 championship season. This year's group, which lost only senior Meghan Lowe, has already eclipsed that number with 10 games left to play.

And the Wilkowskis are leading the way.

Grace, a sophomore, is averaging 17.6 points and 13.3 rebounds a game. In her last three games, she scored 29, 22 and 29 points.

"It's like watching a ballet," Kunst said. "She never makes a mistake. She never gets flustered. Her experience almost never changes the whole game."

Her sister, Mary, is boisterous and vocal on the court. Grace described her as reliable, aggressive and a "dominating presence" in a game.

Their work as a pair on the court is also evident.

The girls have played basketball together since their childhood days in Charlottesville, Va. Less than one year apart in age, they graduated to organized ball at the YMCA in elementary school before moving to Savannah.

"We complement each other really well on the court," Grace said. "We play really well together."

Their teammates know it.

"The girls who are playing with Mary and Grace, they know they are playing with something special," Kunst said.

They also know what's coming next year.

Another sister.

St. Andrew's eighth-grader Rose Wilkowski is slated to advance to the varsity next season.

"All three will probably start next year, which will be interesting," Kunst said.

School: St. Andrew's

Who: Mary, 5-11 freshman
School: St. Andrew's

Author: Donald Heath
Summary: Donald Heath covered St. Andrew's 60-49 championship win over W.W. King, including the second-half comeback, Meghan Miller's fourth-quarter burst, the Wilkowski sisters' scoring, and the net-cutting celebration in Sumter.

King led 29-24 at halftime behind Kerianne Blease, but St. Andrew's pressed more aggressively, controlled the boards, and outscored the Knights 36-20 after halftime.

Title: GIRLS' HIGH SCHOOL PREVIEW 2005: HARDWOOD HEROINES - GRACE, MARY AND ROSE WILKOWSKI TOP LIST OF AREA PLAYERS TO WATCH
Subtitle: A preseason feature on the Wilkowski sisters and St. Andrew's place among the SCISA Class AA favorites.
Author: Donald Heath
Summary: Donald Heath's 2005 Savannah Morning News preview centered on Grace, Mary, and Rose Wilkowski as three distinct sisters whose shared basketball talent made St. Andrew's the overwhelming favorite to repeat as SCISA Class AA champion.
SourceCitation: Donald Heath, "GIRLS' HIGH SCHOOL PREVIEW 2005: HARDWOOD HEROINES - GRACE, MARY AND ROSE WILKOWSKI TOP LIST OF AREA PLAYERS TO WATCH," Savannah Morning News (GA), November 19, 2005, Page 1D.
ArchiveNote: This archive page preserves citation details and an original summary. The full newspaper text is not republished here.
Transcript:
Donald Heath's preseason feature presented Grace, Mary, and Rose Wilkowski as the centerpiece of the 2005-06 St. Andrew's girls basketball story. The article used classroom and practice details to distinguish the sisters' personalities: Grace as thoughtful and college-minded, Mary as outgoing and direct, and Rose as a younger sister with her own offbeat energy.

On the court, the preview described the three sisters as similar in size, shot profile, and movement without the ball, while emphasizing how naturally they played together. Grace entered her senior season after averaging roughly 17 points and 10 rebounds per game. Mary and Rose were each described as double-figure scorers and rebounders, giving St. Andrew's three returning frontcourt anchors.

The article also placed the sisters within a larger family and program context. Their father, Michael Wilkowski, had played college basketball at Carleton College, and the sisters had grown up playing together before becoming fixtures in the St. Andrew's lineup. Coach Michael Bennet credited much of their basketball feel to driveway games rather than formal instruction.

As a season preview, the story made clear why St. Andrew's entered 2005-06 with championship expectations. The Saints had won the previous two SCISA Class AA basketball titles and had just captured a second straight SCISA Class AA volleyball championship with the Wilkowski sisters contributing. The article framed the new basketball season as a title-defense year built around Grace's record chase, Mary's athletic growth, Rose's rising role, and the pressure of being the expected repeat champion.

Author: Noell Barnidge

Transcript:
ST. ANDREW'S GIRLS LOOKING TO CLIMB THE LADDER AGAIN

Meghan Miller is eager to climb a ladder Saturday at the Sumter County (S.C.) Exhibition Center.

The St. Andrew's senior point guard wants to cut down one of the basketball nets in celebration of a SCISA Class AA state championship.

But before Miller can snip some twine with a pair of scissors, St. Andrew's (20-3) must beat Williamsburg (17-10) at 3:30 p.m. today in the quarterfinals of the SCISA Class AA tournament.

With a win, St. Andrew's would advance to the state semifinals at 3:30 p.m. Friday.

All tournament games will be held at the Exhibition Center.

The state championship game is at 2:30 p.m. Saturday. It would be the Saints' third consecutive trip to the title game, where they lost two seasons ago before winning last season.

"Winning back-to-back state championships would be awesome," Miller said. "It's been our goal all season. Being a senior, I don't want to lose my last game. I want to cut down the net again."

With six seniors graduating, St. Andrew's coach Michael Bennet said the window of opportunity for winning another championship could be closing.

"I was telling them at practice today that every time we get together could be the last," Bennet said. "This is a loaded team. The time is now. We're very deep. I've got nine players I can put on the court and be successful with."

Miller and sophomore guard Megan Hall often are overlooked because of the scoring prowess of their teammates, the Wilkowski sisters - Grace, Mary and Rose.

Grace Wilkowski, a senior, averages a team-high 15 points per game and nine rebounds. Mary Wilkowski, a junior, averages 14 points and a team-high 10 rebounds. Rose Wilkowski, a sophomore, averages 12 points.

But at the Saints' annual awards banquet Monday night, it was Miller who won the team's Most Valuable Player award.

"Everybody focuses so much on Mary, Grace and Rose," Bennet said, "but Meghan is our only point guard and she can really control the game. She's irreplaceable."

Miller said she wasn't expecting the award.

"It was really cool to get, but I don't think of myself as the team's MVP," said Miller. "I think of myself as the point guard whose job is to get the ball to the Wilkowski sisters to score."

Bennet points to the Saints' unselfish play, and their ability to improve their skills, as the reason St. Andrew's is primed for a state title repeat. Last season, for example, St. Andrew's made 20 3-pointers. This season, the Saints have made 68 3-pointers.

"Going into this season, I was looking at five or six losses as being successful," Bennet said. "I was looking at 18-5 as a success, and we ended up going 20-3 in the regular season, so we exceeded our expectations. Of our three losses, two were to Hilton Head Prep and the other loss was to Ashley Hall out of Charleston."

Today, St. Andrew's will focus on shutting down Williamsburg center Aynsley Burrell, who averages 14 points and nine rebounds per game. The Saints also plan to continue doing what got them this far, and resulted in a climb up the ladder last season.

"If we just have confidence and play our game, and not get overwhelmed," Miller said, "we can definitely be there on Saturday."

Title: Champs on Campus
Subtitle: A Savannah Morning News opinion piece recognizing St. Andrew's girls basketball and Beach boys basketball after their championship-weekend runs.
Summary: A March 7, 2006 Savannah Morning News opinion piece praised St. Andrew's for repeating as SCISA Class AA champion under the weight of high expectations and recognized the Saints' six seniors for leaving a championship legacy.
SourceCitation: "CHAMPS ON CAMPUS," Savannah Morning News (GA), March 7, 2006, Page 6A, Opinion.
Transcript:
CHAMPS ON CAMPUS

ONE SAVANNAH high school basketball team prevailed under the pressure of high expectations. Another prospered in the absence of such lofty goals, gaining so much with so little to lose.

In our minds, both are champions.

The St. Andrew's girls, led by six senior players, won their second consecutive SCISA Class AA title by defeating Trinity Collegiate last Saturday in Sumter, S.C. For some Saints, the victory produced a collective sigh of relief - they acknowledged the pressure of a veteran team defending its crown.

The Beach boys fell one game short of a GHSA Class AAAAA championship, falling to third-ranked Norcross in the state final Friday night in Duluth. But by then, the Bulldogs had already made a name for themselves with an improbable postseason run.

Underdog Beach, which lost in the semifinals of its region tournament, suddenly got its groove back in the state playoffs by defeating three ranked teams. That included an upset of Wheeler, ranked No. 1 in the state and No. 7 in the nation.

And then there was perhaps the sweetest victory of all, over arch-rival Savannah High, which had defeated Beach three times earlier this season.

St. Andrew's did what most people, including the Saints themselves, knew they could do. Beach accomplished what few believed could happen. Each team proved something to itself, which is often more satisfying than impressing outside observers.

The Saints' six seniors went out with a bang, having established their legacy at the school. The Bulldogs' 10 underclassmen have put everyone on notice for next season: Don't underestimate Beach. The expectations for each just switched.

Title: St. Andrew's Saints - 2005-2006 SCISA Class AA Champs: A Family on and off the Court
Subtitle: Chris Lancia's post-championship feature on St. Andrew's senior class, the Wilkowski sisters, the Griffin twins, and the program legacy after a second straight SCISA Class AA title.
Author: Chris Lancia
Summary: Chris Lancia's March 8, 2006 Savannah Morning News feature looked back at the St. Andrew's girls basketball program after its repeat SCISA Class AA championship, tracing the senior class back to its middle-school roots and emphasizing the team's family feel, Grace Wilkowski's record-setting career, and Michael Bennet's expectation that the Saints would keep contending.
SourceCitation: Chris Lancia, "ST. ANDREW'S SAINTS - 2005-2006 SCISA CLASS AA CHAMPS A FAMILY ON AND OFF THE COURT," Savannah Morning News (GA), March 8, 2006, Page 6D, Sports.
Transcript:
ST. ANDREW'S SAINTS - 2005-2006 SCISA CLASS AA CHAMPS A FAMILY ON AND OFF THE COURT

Six years ago, the sixth-grade girls' basketball team at St. Andrew's made quite an impression, winning the Savannah Parochial Athletic League title.

Their success prompted folks around the Wilmington Island school to wonder how good those girls would be in high school.

Saturday, the St. Andrew's girls' varsity high school basketball team put their final touches to the answer - unbelievably good.

Their second straight South Carolina Independent School Association Class AA title gives them three in the last four years and sends their six seniors out with quite a bit of jewelry.

"We knew back in November that we had the chance to make history - no basketball team at St. Andrew's, boys' or girls', had ever repeated as champs," said coach Michael Bennet. "But I first saw these girls in the seventh and eighth grade, and I thought then that we might have something special here."

Having played together for the better part of a decade, the six seniors on the roster have become more than just a team - they've turned it into a family.

That's not just a clever saying - the Saints have a group of three sisters (Grace, Mary and Rose Wilkowski) and a set of twins (Michelle and Stephanie Griffin) on the roster.

Knowing how tight a group he had, Bennet took a gamble this season by not naming captains. His instincts told him this group would step up.

His instincts were right on. Before each game, the girls decided who to send out to the captains' meeting at half court.

In practice, one of the seniors always seemed to speak up and try to explain things to the younger players.

And in games, he had several coaches on the court.

Having six seniors helps the coach look good during the season - and pull his hair out once it's over.

"Obviously, we're losing a lot of talent because half of our players are seniors," Bennet said. "The hardest thing to replace is the experience. But you can't replace a player like Grace Wilkowski."

Grace finished her basketball career with a school-record 2,017 points and more than 1,000 rebounds. This season she averaged 14.3 points and nine rebounds per game.

Her success didn't disrupt the team chemistry for two reasons: the team accepted her as one of the focal points of their offense, and she deflected as much attention as she could to her teammates.

"She doesn't want the attention, and she'd rather let someone else be in the spotlight," said Bennet. "If any of the three Wilkowski sisters had a 'me first' attitude, I believe it would have affected the chemistry of the team. But they don't, so there's no jealousy or resentment because they try to stay low key and share the attention."

This year's success has helped set the bar high for future classes - the expectation is to be playing in the last game of the season every year.

While losing six players will take a toll, the Saints have a chance at a three-peat.

"We've got a good group to build around coming back, and some good young players coming up from the JV team who are ready to step up," said Bennet. "They'll have some good players coming back that they can learn from, and I like having that progression, where the pressure isn't on them right away and they can take the time to develop."

A realignment of the regions in SCISA means a tougher road to the title next year, as there will be 30 Class AA teams instead of the current 18.

But the Saints still consider themselves the favorites.

"Every team should aspire to be playing in the championship game each year, and this team knows how to get there," Bennet said. "Our girls know it will be a challenge to get there, but we expect to be there on the last Saturday of the season. That's always the goal."

SENIOR SPEAK

"It's like a fairy tale. In middle school, we had people telling us we'd be awesome during our senior year, so winning the state title as a senior is a big deal. It was a wonderful feeling to share it with this group." - Kristen Albritton

"We beat the No. 1 GISA team, Pinewood, this season, and that was awesome. But the weirdest thing was everyone coming up to me on Saturday and congratulating me on a good career, because it hasn't sunk in yet that it's over."- Meghan Miller

"When I first started at St. Andrew's, I never thought I'd be a part of a team that would win back-to-back championships, certainly not in basketball. So this is just a great feeling."- Michelle Griffin

"This was our last year, and you want to go out the right way, so there's a lot of pressure. But we trust each other a lot, and we might as well all be sisters, so I could not have asked to go out a better way." - Emily Aimone

"We like - no, we love each other - and we've got such a bond in this group of seniors. This was a perfect way to end the season."- Stephanie Griffin

"There's nothing better than winning your last game - you can't do better than that. I couldn't ask for a better group of seniors to do it with." - Grace Wilkowski
